sections.title: II.A. Human Factors
sections.content:
II.A. Human Factors
References:
Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25); Chapter 17 pgs. 1-19
Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3) Chapter5 pg. 3
AIM – Chapter 8
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
Safety in the aircraft requires knowledge of the factors that can lead to negative consequences if we were unaware or unable to treat them. Hypoxia, for example, can result in symptoms of euphoria and the inability to make any sort of rational decision, which is obviously not a good thing while you’re trying to fly a plane. (There are many good hyperbaric chamber/hypoxia videos on you tube)
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Human factors involve several health and physiological factors that can influence a pilot and his or her ability to fly safely. Some are minor, while others require special attention to ensure safety and survival.
Why
Many of these factors not only affect the health and well-being of the pilot but can quickly lead to in-flight emergencies.
How:
Hypoxia 												AI.II.A.K1a
Hypoxia means “reduced oxygen” or “not enough oxygen”
The greatest concern is getting oxygen to the brain, since it is particularly vulnerable to oxygen deprivation
Hypoxia can be caused by several factors including:
An insufficient supply of oxygen
Inadequate transportation of oxygen
Inability of the body tissues to use oxygen
Hypoxic Hypoxia
A result of insufficient oxygen available to the lungs
A blocked airway or drowning are examples of how the lungs can be deprived of oxygen
For Pilots: The reduction in partial pressure of oxygen at high altitude is a common example
Partial Pressure: amount of pressure that a single gas (out of a mixture) contributes to the total pressure
Although the percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere is constant with changes in altitude, partial pressure decreases as altitude increases
As you ascend, the percentage of each gas remains the same, but the molecules no longer have the pressure required to drive oxygen into the respiratory system
The decrease of oxygen molecules at sufficient pressure leads to hypoxic hypoxia
Hypemic Hypoxia
Occurs when the blood is not able to take up and transport sufficient oxygen to the cells in the body
Hypemic means “not enough blood”
This type of hypoxia is a result of oxygen deficiency in the blood
Possible Causes:
Not enough blood volume
Can be caused by severe bleed or blood donation
Certain blood diseases, such as anemia
Hemoglobin, the molecule that transports oxygen, is unable to bind oxygen molecules
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Stagnant Hypoxia
Stagnant means “not flowing;” stagnant hypoxia results when the oxygen rich blood in the lungs isn’t moving to the tissues that need it
Ex. An arm or leg “falling asleep” because the blood flow has been restricted
This type of hypoxia can result from:
Shock
The heart failing to pump blood effectively
A constricted artery
During flight, stagnant hypoxia can occur when pulling excessive positive Gs
Cold temperatures can also decrease the blood supplied to extremities
Histotoxic Hypoxia
The inability of the cells to effectively use oxygen
“Histo” refers to tissues or cells, and “Toxic” means poison
In this case, oxygen is being transported to the cells, but they are unable to use it
Causes:
Alcohol and other drugs, such as narcotics and poison
Drinking an ounce of alcohol is equivalent to an additional 2,000’ of altitude
Symptoms of Hypoxia
The first symptoms are euphoria and a carefree feeling. With increased oxygen starvation, the extremities become less responsive and flying becomes less coordinated.
As it worsens, vision narrows, concentration and instrument interpretation become difficult
Common symptoms include:
Cyanosis (blue fingernails and lips)
Headache
Delayed reactions
Impaired judgment
Euphoria
Visual Impairment
Drowsiness
Lightheaded or dizzy sensation
Tingling in fingers or toes
Numbness
Even with all of these symptoms, the effects of hypoxia can cause a pilot to have a false sense of security and be deceived into believing that everything is normal (euphoria)
Useful Consciousness
Describes the maximum time the pilot has to make rational, lifesaving decisions and carry them out at a given altitude without supplemental oxygen
Above 10,000 ft., symptoms increase in severity, and time of useful consciousness rapidly decreases
Treatment
Flying at lower altitudes (Emergency Descent)
Use supplemental oxygen immediately
FAA Physiology Training – One day course in OK. Altitude chamber and vertigo demonstrations
Experiencing and witnessing the effects of hypoxia can be very helpful to recognizing its onset
Hyperventilation 											AI.II.A.K1b
Occurs when experiencing emotional stress, fright, or pain, and the breathing rate and depth increase
Result is an excessive loss of carbon dioxide from the body, which can lead to unconsciousness while the respiratory system attempts to override your actions and regain control of breathing
Pilots encountering a stressful situation may unconsciously increase their breathing rate
At higher altitudes, with or without oxygen, a pilot may tend to breathe more rapidly than normal, which can lead to hyperventilation
Hyperventilation symptoms are similar to hypoxia so it’s important to treat the proper condition
Common Symptoms:
Visual Impairment
Unconsciousness
Lightheaded or dizzy sensation
Tingling sensations
Hot and cold sensations
Muscle spasms
Treatment
Involves restoring the proper carbon dioxide level in the body
If using supplemental oxygen, check the equipment and flow rate to ensure it’s not hypoxia
If unsure, hypoxia is the more threatening situation and should be treated
Breathing normally is the best prevention and the best cure for hyperventilation
Breathing into a paper bag or talking aloud helps
Recovery is usually rapid once breathing is returned to normal
Middle Ear and Sinus Problems 									AI.II.A.K1c
Middle Ear Problems
Explanation
Difference between the outside air pressure and the air inside the middle ear and nasal sinuses
The middle ear is a small cavity located in the bone of the skull

sections.title: Normally, the pressure differences are equalized by the Eust
sections.content:
Normally, the pressure differences are equalized by the Eustachian Tube
A tube leading from inside each ear to the back of the throat on each side
Tubes are usually closed, but open with chewing, yawning or swallowing to equalize pressure
Symptoms
Pain is the primary indicator
Large pressure differences can lead to excessive pain and eardrum damage
Temporary reduction in hearing sensitivity
Relation to flying
Climb: Eardrum bulges outward as pressure in the eustachian tube remains the same while outside air pressure decreases, resulting in discomfort
Descent: Eardrum bulges inward causing discomfort as outside pressure increases while pressure in the Eustachian tube remains at altitude
Excessive pressure in either situation can result in pain and a ruptured ear drum
Treatment
If minor, chew gum or stretch the jaw to attempt to equalize pressure
Pinch the nostrils, close the mouth, and blow slowly and gently in the mouth and nose
Forces air into the Eustachian tube allowing the pressure to equalize
May not be possible to equalize the pressure with a cold, an ear infection, or sore throat
Be cautious in a climb, forcing air into the Eustachian tube can add more pressure and force the eardrum farther outward leading to increased pain
If experiencing minor congestion, nose drops, or nasal sprays may reduce painful ear blockage
Sinus Problems
Explanation
Air pressure in the sinuses equalizes with the pressure in the flight deck through small openings that connect the sinuses to the nasal passages
An upper respiratory infection (cold or sinusitis) or a nasal allergic condition can produce enough congestion to slow equalization
Symptoms
Pain over the sinus area (pain can become excessive)
Some sinus blocks can make the upper teeth ache
Bloody mucus may discharge from the nasal passages
Relation to flying
As the difference in pressure increases, congestion may plug the sinus’ openings
“Sinus block” occurs most frequently during descents
Treatment
Use slow descent rates
Do not fly with sinus problems
Spatial Disorientation 										AI.II.A.K1d
Explanation
Orientation: The awareness of the position of the aircraft and of oneself in relation to a specific reference point
Spatial Disorientation refers to the lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude, or movement of the airplane in space
The body uses three systems to ascertain orientation and movement in space
Visual: The eye, by far the largest source of information
Somatosensory: Nerves in the skin, muscles, and joints that, along with hearing, sense position based on gravity, feeling, and sound
Vestibular System: A very sensitive motion sensing system located in the inner ears
Reports head position, orientation, and movement in 3-dimensional space
When all 3 systems agree you have a clear idea of where and how the body is moving
When they don’t agree is when you become disoriented
Relation to flight
Flying can result in conflicting information being sent to the brain, leading to disorientation
Visual System (eyes)
Flight in VMC
Eyes are the major orientation system and can usually prevail over false sensations
Flight in IMC
Without visual cues, the eyes can’t correct for false sensations which leads to disorientation
Vestibular System (inner ear)
Allows the pilot to sense movement and determine orientation in the surrounding environment
Two major parts: Semicircular Canals and Otolith Organs
Semicircular Canals
Explanation
Detect angular acceleration
Three tubes at right angles to each other (one on each axis)
Each canal is filled with Endolymph Fluid
In the center of the canal is the cupola
Gelatinous structure resting on sensory hairs at the end of the vestibular nerves
How they work: In a Turn
Turn Detection
Unaccelerated, Straight & Level Flight
Hair cells are upright, and the brain doesn’t sense a turn
Turning Flight
Semicircular canal and its fluid are put into motion
Fluid lags behind the canal walls
Canal wall and cupola move in the opposite direction of the fluid
Brain interprets the hair movement as a turn
Only detects turns of a short duration
After about 20 seconds, the fluid catches up with the canal walls and the hairs are no longer bent (unaccelerated, straight & level flight)
Hairs detect no relative movement so the sensation of turning ceases
Returning to straight-and-level flight, the fluid moves in the opposite direction
Falsely interpreted as a turn in the opposite direction
To correct for this, the pilot reenters the original turn
Demonstration: Establish a 30o bank turn, tell the student to close their eyes and let you know when the aircraft is flying straight. Try it again, but this time once they believe the aircraft is straight, roll out of the bank. The student will feel like the aircraft is turning in the opposite direction.
Otolith Organs
Explanation
Detect linear acceleration/gravity
A gelatinous membrane containing chalk like crystals covers the sensory hairs
When you tilt your head, the weight of the crystals causes the membrane to shift due to gravity and sensory hairs detect the shift
Acceleration
Forward acceleration gives the illusion of the head tilting backward and deceleration gives the illusion of the head tilting forward
Somatosensory System (nerves)
Nerves in the body’s skin, muscles, and joints constantly send signals to the brain which signals the body’s relation to gravity
Ex. Acceleration will be felt as the pilot is pushed back into the seat
False Sensations
Forces created in turns can lead to false sensations of the direction of gravity
The brain cannot differentiate between the forces of a turn and the force of gravity
Turbulence can create motions that confuse the brain
Fatigue or illness can exacerbate these sensations
Countering the sensations
Recognize the problem, disregard the false sensations, and rely totally on the flight instruments
Understand the problem and control the aircraft using only instrument indications
Motion Sickness 											AI.II.A.K1e
Cause
Caused by the brain receiving conflicting messages about the state of the body
Anxiety and stress also affect motion sickness
Symptoms
General discomfort
Nausea
Dizziness
Paleness
Sweating
Vomiting
Treatment

sections.title: Open fresh air vents
sections.content:
Open fresh air vents
Focus on objects outside the airplane
Avoid unnecessary head movement
Take control of the aircraft and fly smooth, straight and level
Letting someone else fly can make the situation worse
Usually goes away after a few flight lessons
More used to flying and stress/anxiety are reduced
Carbon Monoxide Poisoning 									AI.II.A.K1f
How it Happens – In the Plane
Carbon Monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas produced by all internal combustion engines
If the exhaust system is damaged or leaking, heat/defrost vents can provide CO a way into the cabin
How it Happens – In the Body
CO attaches itself to the hemoglobin in the blood
It does this about 200 times easier than oxygen
CO prevents the hemoglobin from carrying oxygen to the cells resulting in Hypemic Hypoxia
Can take up to 48 hours for the body to dispose of CO
If severe enough, CO poisoning can result in death
Effects of CO poisoning
Headache
Blurred vision
Dizziness
Drowsiness
Loss of muscle power
Detecting and Correction
Disposable, inexpensive CO detectors are widely available
If a strong odor of exhaust gases is detected, assume CO is present
CO may be present in dangerous amounts even if no exhaust odor is detected
If exhaust odor is noticed or symptoms are experienced, immediate actions should be taken
Turn off the heater
Open fresh air vents and windows
Use supplemental oxygen, if available
Land
Fatigue and Stress
Fatigue 												AI.II.A.K1h
Effects
Degradation of attention and concentration
Impaired coordination
Decreased ability to communicate
Causes
Sleep loss
Exercise
Physical work
Stress and prolonged performance of cognitive work can result in mental fatigue
Categories of Fatigue (Acute and Chronic)
Acute Fatigue (short term)
Definition
Short term, and a normal occurrence in everyday life
Tiredness felt after a period of strenuous effort, excitement, or lack of sleep
Skill Fatigue – A special type of acute fatigue affecting piloting skill. Effects include:
Timing Disruption
Appearing to perform a normal task, but the timing of each component is slightly off
Pattern of operation is less smooth as each component is performed as a separate part instead of part of a single, integrated activity
Disruption of the perceptual field
Concentrating attention upon movements or objects in the center of vision and neglecting those in the periphery
May be accompanied by a loss of accuracy/smoothness in control movements
Causes
Mild hypoxia
Physical stress
Psychological stress
Depletion of physical energy resulting from psychological stress
Sustained psychological stress
Prevention
Proper diet
Prevents the body from having to consume its own tissues as an energy source
Adequate rest and sleep
Maintains the body’s store of vital energy
The difference between flying fatigued and rested can be night and day,
Chronic Fatigue
Definition
Fatigue extending over a long period of time
Usually has psychological roots, an underlying disease is sometimes responsible
Causes
Continuous high-stress levels produce chronic fatigue
Symptoms
Weakness
Tiredness
Palpitations of the heart
Breathlessness
Headaches
Irritability
Stomach or intestinal problems (rare)
Generalized aches and pains throughout the body
Emotional Illness (when conditions become serious enough)
Prevention
Usually requires treatment by a physician
Prevention
If suffering from acute fatigue, stay on the ground
Fatigue in the flight deck cannot be overcome through training or experience
Getting adequate rest is the only way to prevent fatigue
Avoid flying
Without a full night’s rest
After working excessive hours
After an especially exhausting or stressful day
Suspected chronic fatigue should be treated by a physician
Stress 												AI.II.A.K1g
Body’s response to physical and psychological demands placed upon it
Body’s Reaction
Releasing chemical hormones (such as adrenaline) into the blood
Increasing metabolism to provide more energy to the muscles
Blood sugar, heart rate, respiration, blood pressure, and perspiration all increase
Stressors (elements that cause an individual to experience stress)
Physical stress (noise or vibration)
Physiological stress (fatigue)
Psychological stress (difficult work or personal situations)
Categories of Stress (Acute and Chronic)
Acute Stress (short term)

sections.title: Involves an immediate threat that is perceived as danger
sections.content:
Involves an immediate threat that is perceived as danger
The type of stress that triggers a “fight or flight” response in an individual
Normally, a healthy person can cope with acute stress and prevent stress overload
On-going acute stress can develop into chronic stress
Chronic Stress (long term)
Presents an intolerable burden, exceeds the ability to cope, causes performance to fall sharply
Causes
Unrelenting psychological pressures
Ex. Loneliness, financial worries, and relationship or work problems
Do not fly. Consult a physician
Dehydration & Nutrition										 AI.II.A.K1i
Dehydration
Critical loss of water from the body
Causes
Hot flight decks/flight lines, wind, humidity, diuretic drinks (coffee, tea, alcohol, caffeinated soda)
Effects
First noticeable effect is fatigue
Top physical and mental performance is difficult, if not impossible
Headache, cramps, tingling, sleepiness, and dizziness
How it affects flying
Hot temperatures and high altitudes increase susceptibility to dehydration
Dry air at altitude increases the body’s rate of water loss
Fatigue progresses to dizziness, weakness, nausea, tingling hands & feet, abdominal cramps, and extreme thirst
Attention is taken from flying and skills diminish
Prevention
Carry an ample supply of water (recommended to drink 2 quarts of water per day)
Stay ahead – don’t wait until you’re thirsty to drink
Wear light colored, porous clothing and a hat
Keep the flight deck well ventilated
Limit caffeine and alcohol intake
Nutrition
Ensure properly fed and nourished
Causes: Missing/postponing meals and/or poor eating habits
Effects
Low energy and/or low blood sugar
Stomach contractions, distraction, breakdown in habit patterns, and shortened attention span
Insufficient vitamin A can impair night vision
Prevention: Eat healthy, regularly spaced and sized meals
Hypothermia 											AI.II.A.K1j
How it Happens
The body loses heat faster than it can be produced
Normal body temperature is 98.6o F (37o C), hypothermia occurs below 95o F (35o C)
Mechanisms of heat loss
Radiated heat: Most heat loss is due to heat radiated from unprotected parts of the body
Direct contact: In contact with something very cold, heat is conducted away from the body
Heat is lost much faster in cold water than cold air
Heat loss if much faster if clothes are wet
Wind: Carries away the thin layer of warm air at the surface of your skin
Causes
Clothes that aren’t warm enough for the weather
Too much time in the cold
Falling into cold water
Unable to get out of wet clothes or move to a warm, dry location
Symptoms
Shivering
Slurred speech or mumbling
Slow, shallow breathing
Weak pulse
Clumsiness
Drowsiness
Confusion or memory loss (can prevent the person from knowing they have hypothermia)
Bright red, cold skin
Prevention (COLD)
Cover: Wear protective clothing
Cover your head, face, and neck. Wear mittens instead of gloves
Overexertion
Avoid activities that result in a lot of sweat
Wet clothing + cold weather causes body heat to be lost more quickly
Layers
Loose fitting, layered, lightweight clothing
Wool, silk or polypropylene inner layers hold heat better than cotton
Tightly woven, water repellent material is best for wind protection
Dry
Stay dry – get out of wet clothing as soon as possible
Optical Illusions 											AI.II.A.K1k
Runway Width Illusion
Reason
A narrower than usual runway
A wider than usual runway
Illusion
Narrow: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it is
Wide: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a lower altitude than it is
Result
Narrow: The pilot who doesn’t recognize this will fly a lower approach, with the risk of striking objects along the approach path or landing short
Wide: the pilot who doesn’t recognize this will fly a higher approach, with the risk of leveling out high and landing hard or overshooting the runway
Runway and Terrain Slope Illusion
Reason
An up-sloping runway, up sloping terrain, or both
A down sloping runway, down sloping terrain, or both
Illusion
Upslope: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it is
Downslope: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a lower altitude than it is
Result
Upslope: The pilot who does not recognize this will fly a lower approach
Downslope: The pilot who does not recognize this will fly a higher approach
Featureless Terrain Illusion
Reason
An absence of ground features, as when landing over water, darkened areas, and terrain made featureless by snow
Illusion
Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it is
Result
The pilot who doesn’t recognize this will fly a lower approach
Atmospheric Illusions
Reason
Rain on the windscreen
Atmospheric Haze

sections.title: Penetration of fog
sections.content:
Penetration of fog
Illusion
Rain - Can create the illusion of greater height
Atmospheric Haze: Can create the illusion of being a greater distance from the runway
Penetration of Fog: Can create the illusion of pitching up
Result
Rain & Haze: The pilot who does not recognize these illusions will fly a lower approach
Fog: The pilot who does not recognize this will steepen the approach, often quite abruptly
Ground Lighting Illusions
Reason: Lights along a straight path, such as a road, and even lights on moving trains
Illusions: Can create the illusion of runway and approach lights
Result: The pilot may attempt to land on a path, road, or train
Reason: Bright runway and approach lighting systems
Illusion: Can create the illusion of less distance to the runway
Especially where few lights illuminate the surrounding terrain
Result: The pilot who does not recognize this illusion will fly a higher approach
Preventing Landing Illusions
Anticipate them during approaches
Aerial visual inspection of unfamiliar airports before landing
Using glide slope or VASI/PAPI systems whenever possible
Maintaining optimum proficiency in landing procedures
Nitrogen and Scuba Diving 										AI.II.A.K1i
Why it’s a Danger
Scuba diving results in a significant increase in the amount of nitrogen dissolved in the body
The deeper the dive, the greater the nitrogen
At sea level, the nitrogen inside and outside the body is in equilibrium
When atmospheric pressure is reduced, nitrogen leaves the body
If the nitrogen leaves too quickly, bubbles may form causing a variety of symptoms
Bubbles can form in the bloodstream, spinal cord or brain
Symptoms include impairment or severe pain - extreme cases can result in death
Scuba Diving and Flying
If enough time isn’t provided, DCS can occur as low as 5,000’ and create an in-flight emergency
In normal conditions, most cases of DCS occur at altitudes of 25,000’ or higher
Wait at least 12 hrs. after a dive not requiring a controlled ascent before flight up to 8,000’ MSL
24 hrs. for flight above 8,000’
Wait at least 24 hrs. after a dive that requires a controlled ascent before flight up to 8,000’ MSL
If a decompression occurs, DCS symptoms can be brought on quickly
Alcohol and Other Drugs 									AI.II.A.K2. AI.II.A.K3
DON’T drink and fly
Even in small amounts, alcohol can impair judgement, decrease sense of responsibility, affect coordination, constrict visual field, diminish memory, reduce reasoning ability, lower attention span
Altitude multiplies the effects of alcohol on the brain
Alcohol interferes with the brains ability to utilize oxygen (form of histotoxic hypoxia)
A hangover can impair anyone attempting to fly
FAR 91.17 – 8 hrs. ‘from bottle to throttle’ (8 hrs. and not feeling the effects of alcohol is better)
Considerable amounts of alcohol can remain in the body for over 16 hours – be cautious
Medications
FAR 61.53 (Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency) prohibits flying if you:
Are taking medication/receiving treatment that would prevent you from obtaining a medical
FAR 91.17 prohibits use of drugs affecting a person’s faculties in any way contrary to safety
Medication can absolutely affect pilot performance
Side effects can impair judgment, memory, alertness, coordination, vision, can cause confusion, dizziness, headaches, nausea, mood swings, anxiety, balance problems, hearing problems, etc.
Drugs that cause no apparent side effects on the ground can create serious problems airborne
Basically: Do not fly while taking any medication(s), unless approved by the FAA
ADM, CRM, & SRM 											AI.II.A.K4
RM: Distractions (Task Prioritization, Loss of SA, Disorientation) 					AI.II.A.R3
Human factors can present significant, distractions, disorientation, and an inability to manage tasks
The pilot must perform an honest evaluation of themselves prior to flight
IMSAFE:
Illness – Symptoms?
Medication – Taking any?
Stress – Family, money, relationships, work, etc.
Alcohol – Been drinking?
Fatigue – Well rested?
Emotion – Emotionally upset?
In flight, be alert to factors that can affect performance and lead to disorientation, etc.
RM: Combat confirmation/expectation bias 							AI.II.A.R4
Your expectations can influence behavior
Individuals are vulnerable to thinking they see (or hear) what they expect to see (or hear)
Don’t assume everything will be OK, because it’s always been OK
If something doesn’t feel right (i.e., hypoxia symptoms), take action
Stress Management
Learning to cope with stress is an effective ADM tool
A certain amount of stress is good – keeps you alert and prevents complacency
Stress is cumulative, too much can amount to an intolerable burden
Performance increases with the onset of stress, peaks, then falls rapidly as stress gets too high
Stressors can increase risk of error
Physical: Associated with the environment (temperature, noise, vibration, lack of oxygen)
Physiological: Physical conditions (fatigue, lack of physical fitness, missed meals)
Psychological: Social or emotional factors (divorce, death in the family, sick child)
Recognize when stress affect performance
RM: Hazardous Attitudes 									AI.II.A.R2
Attitude affects the quality of decisions
5 hazardous attitudes that can interfere with the ability to make sound decisions
Contribute to poor judgement
Recognizing is the first step to neutralizing these attitudes
Once recognizing a thought as hazardous, label it as hazardous and state the antidote
Attitudes & Antidotes
Use all Resources
Use all available resources – Don’t depend solely on yourself
Internal Resources
Equipment (autopilot, GPS, etc.), systems, charts, books, etc.
Ingenuity, knowledge, and skill
Other passengers (even if they are not pilots)
External Resources
ATC, FSS, Guard, etc. (Traffic advisories, vectors, weather info, emergency assistance)
Workload Management
Plan, prioritize, and sequence to prevent overload
Prepare for high workload situations
Don’t wait until you’re in the situation (i.e., prepare for the approach before it begins)
Be able to recognize high workloads
Faster paced work along with divided attention
Stay ahead as much as possible to prevent high workloads
Manage tasks in order of importance when behind
“Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing/threatening issue
RM: Aeromedical & Physiological Issues 								AI.II.A.R2
The lesson as a whole is a discussion of managing risk associated with aeromedical issues

sections.title: Conclusion:
sections.content:
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
There are many factors a pilot needs to be aware of to ensure a safe flight and to understand the medical risks involved with flying. Recognize conditions and symptoms associated with physiological issues and take action to maintain safety, whether that means supplemental oxygen, trusting the instruments, or diverting and landing as soon as possible.

keyTakeaways: Middle Ear and Sinus Problems 									AI.II.A.K1c
Alcohol and Other Drugs 									AI.II.A.K2. AI.II.A.K3

sections.title: V.B. Flight Deck Management
sections.content:
V.B. Flight Deck Management
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
All pilots need to learn to be good housekeepers. The airplane is your house, and you need to be sure it stays clean and organized.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Flight deck management (single pilot resource management) is a process that combines you, the airplane, and the environment for safer and more efficient operations.
Why
Understanding the elements behind flight deck management (single pilot resource management) provides for a considerably more efficient and safer flight.
How:
Passenger Briefing 											AI.V.B.K1
Safety Belts
FAR 91.107 - Each person must be briefed on how to fasten and unfasten their safety belt/shoulder harness
Cannot taxi, takeoff, land without ensuring each person has fastened their safety belt/shoulder harness
Briefing Topics
Combination of FAR 91.519 (Briefing requirements for Turbine-Powered Multiengine Airplanes and Fractional Aircraft), FAASafety Passenger Briefing and common topics
Identify the PIC
Safety belts and harnesses
Exits (how to operate the doors and emergency exits_
Additional pertinent emergency procedures
Fire extinguishers
Specific exit procedures, if necessary
Avoiding propeller blades
Gathering point in case of an evacuation
Passenger Conduct
Talking (i.e. sterile flight deck/not during taxi, takeoff, landing unless safety requires it)
See and avoid (pointing out other aircraft)

sections.title: Location of survival equipment
sections.content:
Location of survival equipment
Ditching procedures/flotation equipment
Systems
Use of oxygen systems (normal and/or emergency)
Heat/Air
No smoking
Questions
FAASafety passenger briefing discussion and briefing card – Passenger Briefing
Arranging & Securing 										AI.V.B.K4
Arranging
Ensure that all the necessary equipment, documents, checklists & navigation charts are on board
Materials should be neatly arranged and organized to make them readily available for use
Any equipment with wires should not interfere with the motion or operation of any controls
Securing
Secure all cargo to prevent movement during flight
Loose cargo could be hazardous to people and/or aircraft CG/balance
Check for loose articles which might be tossed about during flight, or in turbulence
Form the habit of “good housekeeping;” in the long run, it will pay off in safe and efficient flying
Seat Position & Controls
Seat Belt/Harnesses
When seated, the seat belt/harness should be adjusted to a comfortable, snug fit
Shoulder harness must be worn at least for taxi, takeoff, and landing
The safety belt must be worn all times at the controls
Seats
On each flight, the pilot should be seated in the same position
Adjust height for the proper viewing height as directed in the POH
The pilot(s) must be able to see inside and outside references
If the seat is adjustable, it is important to ensure that the seat is locked in position
Many accidents have occurred as the result of the seat suddenly moving with acceleration/deceleration
Rudder Pedals
Adjust the rudder pedals forward or backward

sections.title: Knees should be slightly bent
sections.content:
Knees should be slightly bent
With heels on the floor and balls of the feet on the pedals full movement should be available
Using toes, the brakes should be able to be actuated
Navigation Data Currency 										AI.V.B.K3
Charts
FAR 91.103 requires each PIC to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight
Although it doesn’t specifically require it, you should always carry current charts
Information changes rapidly, out of date charts may be missing crucial information
Ex: Changes to airspace, new special airspace, change to procedures, frequencies, etc.
To confirm currency, refer to the next scheduled edition date printed on the cover
Use the FAAs Dates of Latest Editions to verify you have the most current edition
Prior to expiration, check NOTAMs and Safety Alerts and Charting Notices for any changes
Database Currency
AIM 1-1-1b3(b): Databases must be maintained to the current update for IFR operations
No such requirements exist for VFR ops, however it is always a good idea to keep a current database
Violations
It is not FAA policy to initiate enforcement action against a pilot for having an old chart or no chart, or for having an expired navigation database
However, if a pilot is involved in an enforcement investigate and there is evidence that an out-of-date chart/database (or no chart) contributed to the situation, then that information could be used in any enforcement action that might be taken
Bottom line, use current charts/databases
Checklist Usage 											AI.V.B.K2
Ensure the proper and orderly use of the manufacturer’s checklist
Ensures every item is completed and checked in a logical order
Don’t go on memory, always backup your actions with a checklist
Sooner or later, you will make a mistake without a checklist
RM: Inoperative Equipment 									AI.V.B.R2
On the Ground
Perform a thorough preflight
Follow FAR 91.213(d) procedures to defer & placard equipment as inoperative
See III.B. Airworthiness Requirements
There should be no question as to what equipment is or isn’t operative
Consider the effects the inoperative equipment will have on the flight

sections.title: Set and follow personal equipment minimums – just because it
sections.content:
Set and follow personal equipment minimums – just because it’s legal, doesn’t mean it’s safe
Ex: Inflight weather is not required by regs, but it could be hazardous without it on certain days
If you’re not comfortable with the state of the airplane, don’t fly it
Airborne
If equipment becomes inoperative, a decision must be made to continue or divert
Considerations
Would the equipment prevent flying if it happened on the ground? FAR 91.213(d)
How does it affect the remainder of the flight?
How does it affect personal minimums?
If I land somewhere with this inoperative equipment, can I return home?
Other thoughts based on the situation
Resource Utilization
Resources can be found both inside and outside the flight deck. Be aware of all available resources at the pilot’s disposal, and when necessary, think outside the box to get the information/help you need
These resources should be used before, during and after flight
Internal Resources
POH is essential for accurate flight planning and resolving equipment malfunctions
Checklists verify instruments and systems are checked, set, and operating properly and ensure the proper procedures are performed in the case of an emergency
Satellite data, if equipped
App data (such as ForeFlight), if equipped for in-flight updates
Equipment - A thorough understanding of the equipment is necessary to fully utilize all resources
Program any info ahead of time (radio frequencies, fixes, etc.)
If you do not understand equipment, or rely on certain equipment (like GPS) excessively it can be unsafe
Ex: If the GPS fails and you do not have a good understanding of VOR navigation, how will you maintain situation awareness and return home or divert to another field?
Passengers can look for traffic, and provide helpful information (strange sound/scent, checklist help)
Charts, other pilots, and your own ingenuity, knowledge and skill are also excellent resources
External Resources
ATC, maintenance technicians, and flight service personnel
1800 WX Brief
Internet research (before flight – weather, NOTAMs, TFRs, airport procedures, etc.)
ATC/Flight Service specialists can decrease work with traffic advisories, vectors and emergency assistance
May be able to access maintenance personnel, or other assistance in an emergency

sections.title: FSS can provide weather, airport conditions
sections.content:
FSS can provide weather, airport conditions
Other airplanes can provide PIREPs as well as radio communications
Occasionally other aircraft may be able to hear your transmission, but not the controller
In this case, other aircraft can relay messages between you and the controller
ASOS/AWOS can also provide weather conditions in flight
Utilize all available resources during preflight planning as well as during flight
RM: Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Distractions
RM: Passengers Distractions 								AI.V.B.R3
Use the preflight briefing as an opportunity to explain passenger expectations, sterile cockpit, etc.
If a passenger is distracting, explain the situation to them, and ask them to stop
Other Distractions
They’re dangerous, remove them from your view
Don’t allow systems/equipment, people, inoperative systems to distract you from flying the airplane
RM: Automation & PEDs (RM: Use of systems or equipment, including automation & PEDs) 	AI.V.B.R1
Ensure understanding of equipment, systems, automation, electronic devices
Great tools for SA and reduced workload, but a lack of understanding can quickly distract from flying
Over reliance on automation & technology creates an environment where basic airmanship skills are eroded
Understand their operation, use them, but be able to fly proficiently/safely without them
Case Study: Eastern 401
Multi-pilot airplanes have crashed due to minor distractions
Eastern Airlines 401 (December 29, 1972) crashed while the pilots were preoccupied with a light bulb and didn’t realize the autopilot turned off
FAA Lessons Learned
YouTube Video (15 mins)
Risk Management Concepts
Overabundance of technology, loss of SA, distractions, systems understanding & malfunctions, task prioritization
Discuss ways to mitigate these risks
Extremely important in a single pilot aircraft that you divide attention, avoid distraction, and maintain SA
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
By combining all the elements of flight deck management (single pilot resource management), the pilot will have a safer and more efficient flight due to a reduced workload and reduced mental stress and fatigue.

sections.title: V.C. Engine Starting
sections.content:
V.C. Engine Starting
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Reduction of Electrical System Failures Following Aircraft Engine Starting (AC 91-55), Cold Weather Operation of Aircraft - Cancelled (AC 91-13), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
Starting the engine of an airplane is not as simple as starting the engine of your car. A plane can’t just be turned on anywhere at any time, the proper precautions and procedures must be followed for safety reasons.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Engine Starting discusses the safety precautions necessary when starting an airplane, the different conditions which affect starting the engine, as well as different ways to start the engine.
Why
Proper engine starting is necessary for the safety of people and property, as well as to prevent engine damage. There are certain situations which require special procedures, and some procedures can be dangerous. It is very important to know the proper engine starting procedures and precautions.
How:
POH
Always use Manufacturer Checklists
Ensures every item is completed and checked in a logical order
Covers the Before Starting checklist and the Starting Engine Checklists
Especially important with different checklists for varying situations (Flooded, Cold, Normal, Hot, etc.)
Don’t go on memory, always backup your actions with a checklist
Sooner or later you will make a mistake without a checklist
RM: Engine Starting Limitations 								AI.V.C.K3, AI.V.C.R3
Check the Limitations section of the POH for applicable engine start limits
Starter limits, cooling limits between starts, etc.
RM: Safety Precautions (RM: Propeller Safety) 							AI.V.C.R1
Set the parking brake (ensuring they are pumped) and hold the brakes with your toes
Look outside to ensure you are not moving
Too much heads down time (checklists, checking indications, etc.) can result in unrecognized movement and an accident or damage to the aircraft

sections.title: Ensure the ramp area surrounding the airplane is clear of pe
sections.content:
Ensure the ramp area surrounding the airplane is clear of persons, equipment, and other hazards
Be aware of what is in front of, and behind the airplane
Check all directions to ensure nothing is/will be in the vicinity of the propeller, or propeller blast
Propeller thrust can damage to property and injure people
Anti-collision lights should be turned on prior to any start, at night use position lights too
Always call “CLEAR” out of the side window and wait for a response from someone who may be nearby
When activating the starter, the wheel brakes must be depressed
Set the parking brake, if installed (and directed in the POH)
Proper brake application ensures the airplane does not lunge forward upon starting the engine
Keep one hand on the throttle for prompt response if RPM is excessive or a hazardous situation presents itself
Ensure the propeller area is clear of any obstructions (debris, people, obstacles, etc.)
Doublecheck the area behind the aircraft is clear
Engine Starting
Normal Start Checklist
Review the normal start checklist in the POH
Engine Controls During Start
Always keep one hand on the throttle to manage the initial engine starting speed
After the engine is started, set the throttle to the RPM setting specified in the POH
Other controls (mixture, prop, carb heat, boost pump, etc.) should be set/adjusted as specified in the POH/checklist
Monitor the oil pressure after engine start
Ensure the pressure is increasing toward the POH specified value
If normal oil pressure is not reached and maintained, serious internal engine damage is likely
In most conditions, oil pressure should reach at least the lower limit within 30 seconds
If oil pressure does not rise to the POH values in the specified time, shutdown the engine
Check all other instruments to ensure they are operating within limits
Avoid excessive engine RPM and temperatures
Adjust the engine controls to maintain the POH recommended RPM, fuel, propeller, etc. settings
Monitor the instruments and use the checklist if the engine temperature begins to rise abnormally

sections.title: Atmospheric Conditions 									AI.V.C.K1
sections.content:
Atmospheric Conditions 									AI.V.C.K1
Cold Weather
Low temperatures may cause a change in the viscosity of engine oils (they congeal, or become thicker), batteries may lose a higher percentage of their effectiveness, and instruments may stick
Preheat of the engine(s) (and cabin) before starting is desirable
Preheat by storing the airplane in a heated hangar, if possible
Use only heaters that are in good condition and do not refuel the heater while it is operating
Do not leave the aircraft unattended and keep a fire extinguisher handy
Do not place the heat ducting so it will blow hot air directly on combustible parts of the aircraft (upholstery, canvas engine covers, flexible fuel, oil, and hydraulic lines)
Starting the Engine
In moderately cold weather, preheat may not be necessary
Use care, oil may be congealed and turning the engine with the starter or by hand is difficult
If approved by the POH, the pilot may rotate the prop by hand to loosen the congealed oil
Follow the POH procedures, and be positive the engine is OFF to avoid an accidental start
Cold Engine Start Problems
Tendency to overprime, which washes down cylinder walls and may result in scoring of the walls
Also results in poor compression and consequently causes hard starting
Aircraft fires have been started by overpriming
Have a fireguard/extinguisher ready
In a cold engine, icing over the sparkplug electrodes can cause problems
Engine only fires a few revolutions and then quits
Sufficient combustion to cause water in the cylinders, but not enough to heat them up
The water condenses on the sparkplug electrodes, freezes to ice, and shorts them out
Avoid prolonged idling
Engines may quit because sufficient heat is not produced to keep the plugs from fouling out
The only remedy is heat
If a heater is not available, the plugs should be removed from the engine and heated to the point where no moisture is present
Starting
Prime the engine with fuel first (over-priming can result in an aircraft fire – AC 91-13)

sections.title: AC 91-13 is still available to read but has been cancelled a
sections.content:
AC 91-13 is still available to read but has been cancelled and incorporated into various other ACs
After start, follow the POH procedures to allow the engine, and engine oil to warm and circulate
As mentioned, engines may quit with long idling
Hot Weather
Hot Start procedures in the POH
Generally, little to no priming is needed, but if the engine doesn’t catch, use minimum priming
In the case of an overprimed engine (common with hot starts), use the flooded start checklist to clear the excess fuel and start the engine
Vapor lock (fuel injected engines)
Fuel delivery lines tend to be on the top of the engine, directly over the cylinder fins
Heat from the engine/outside can boil the fuel out of the lines creating vapor & preventing start
Hot start attempts to purge/minimize the vapor in the system with the fuel boost pump
*Starting with External Power 								AI.V.C.K2, AI.V.C.R2
RM: Ensure proper use and understanding of the external power unit
Follow steps in the owner’s manual
Besides not being able to start the plane, there is the risk of damaging the unit or aircraft systems
In addition to those items in Section 4, Normal Operating Procedures, check the following items:
Caution Lights (EPU) - Illuminated if power is available
During preflight, check that the EPU connector is inserted and secure
Before Engine Starting
Engine Starting Checklist, plus:
EPU Light: ON; EPU Switch: ON; Voltmeter: Check 12 - 14 Volts
Start the engine as normal (Cold/Warm/Flooded)
After Engine Start
Select EPU switch to OFF: EPU light ON
Signal ground crew to pull the EPU cord: EPU light OFF
Master Switch (GEN): OFF and Check Battery Voltage: Approximately 12 volts
Master Switch (GEN) ON and Check Battery Voltage: Approximately 14 volts
GEN warning light: Check OFF

sections.title: RM: Hand Propping Safety (RM: Propeller Safety) 							AI.V.
sections.content:
RM: Hand Propping Safety (RM: Propeller Safety) 							AI.V.C.R1
Basic requirements BEFORE attempting a hand prop
Do not hand prop unless two people, both familiar with hand propping techniques are available
Never allow a person unfamiliar with the controls to occupy the pilot’s seat when hand propping
The person pulling the propeller blades through directs all activity and is in charge of the procedure
Chocks can be an additional precaution, or tie down the tail (Be careful removing them)
The second person must be seated in the plane to ensure the brakes are set, the controls are properly exercised, and to follow the direction of the person pulling the propeller
The ground surface near the prop should be stable and free of debris (otherwise relocate)
Loose gravel, wet grass, mud, etc. might cause the person pulling the prop to slip into the blades
Both participants should discuss the procedure and agree on voice commands and expected action
*Engine Starting Set-up
The fuel system/engine controls (pump, primer, throttle, mixture) should be set for a normal start
Check to ensure the ignition/magneto switch is OFF
The descending prop blade should be rotated to a position slightly above horizontal
The person doing the propping should face blade squarely and stand less than an arm’s length away
Too far away and it would be necessary to lean forward in an unbalanced condition
*Procedures and Commands for Hand Propping
Person out front says, “GAS ON, SWITCH OFF, THROTTLE CLOSED, BRAKES SET”
Person IN ensures - Fuel: ON, Mixture: RICH, Ignition: OFF, Throttle: CLOSED, Brakes SET, and repeats
Person out front checks the brakes by pushing on the prop
Person out front, after pulling the prop through to prime the engine says, “BRAKES AND CONTACT”
Person in the pilot’s seat checks the brakes SET and turns the ignition switch ON, then repeats
The propeller is swung by forcing the blade downward rapidly as hard as possible
Push with the palms
If the blade is gripped tightly with the fingers, the person’s body may be drawn into the propeller blades should the engine misfire and rotate in the opposite direction
If it does not start, the prop should not be moved until certain the ignition/magneto switch is OFF
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

sections.title: Always ensure safety when starting the engine.
sections.content: Always ensure safety when starting the engine.
