sections.title: IX.F. Eights on Pylons
sections.content:
IX.F. Eights on Pylons
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3)
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
The eights on pylons maneuver started in WWI. This maneuver was developed to maintain a constant view of a target, allowing the gunner to destroy a target. A more practical application now, is keeping the wing out of the way for aerial photography.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Eights on Pylons is an advanced maneuver in which the pilot’s attention is directed at maintaining a pivotal position on a selected pylon, with minimum attention inside the flight deck.
The maneuver itself involves flying the airplane in a figure eight path around two selected points, or pylons, on the ground. However, no attempt is made to maintain a uniform distance from the pylon. Instead, the goal is to have an imaginary line that extends from the pilot’s eyes to the pylon. This line must be imagined to always be parallel to the airplane’s lateral axis. Along this line, the airplane appears to pivot as it turns around the pylon. In other words, if a taut string extended from the airplane to the pylon, the string would remain parallel to lateral axis as the airplane turned around the pylon. At no time should the string be at an angle to the lateral axis.
Why 												AI.IX.F.K1
The objective of this maneuver is to develop the ability to maneuver the airplane accurately while dividing one’s attention between the flight path and the selected points on the ground.  Eights on Pylons are extremely helpful in teaching, developing, and testing subconscious control of the airplane.
How:
What is Pivotal Altitude 										AI.IX.F.K3
General Description
A specific altitude at which, for a given groundspeed, the projection of the visual reference line to the pylon appears to pivot
Basically, the pivotal altitude is the altitude which keeps the pylon in the same position on the window (or other aircraft reference, like the wingtip) as the aircraft turns around it
Pivotal altitude varies with groundspeed
The reference line is parallel with the lateral axis of the airplane
*Off the wingtip in the case of the DA20
In a swept wing aircraft, there will be no wing reference, so the point has to be kept in the same position on the window
The same as keeping the pylon in the center of a target on the window (image, left)
When turning at the pivotal altitude, the wingtip appears to be fixed to a single point on the landscape, but at any height other than the pivotal altitude, the wing tip appears to move across the landscape
When turning at a height greater than the pivotal altitude, which is the normal situation in flight, the wingtip appears to move backward over the landscape
When at a height less than pivotal altitude (close to the ground) the wingtip appears to move forward
The Basics 											AI.IX.F.K2, AI.IX.F.K3
Pivotal Altitude is Based on Groundspeed
As groundspeed increases, pivotal altitude increases, vice versa
Pivotal altitude does not change with bank
Distance from the pylon affects the angle of bank (more below)
Since the headings throughout the turns continually vary from directly downwind to directly upwind, the groundspeed will constantly change
This will result in the pivotal altitude varying throughout the maneuver
The pilot must climb or descend to compensate for the changing groundspeed and to maintain the visual reference with the pylon
The change in altitude will depend on how much the wind affects groundspeed
Strong winds create larger changes in altitude than light winds
No wind would result in no change in altitude
Maintaining the Pivotal Altitude References
Pitch
As groundspeed decreases, pivotal altitude decreases
If no changes are made, as the aircraft slows it will be above the pivotal altitude
The wing will appear to move backward across the landscape
The point will move forward in relation to the wing
To compensate, the pilot must descend to maintain the reference line to the pylon
Airspeed increases slightly, increasing pivotal altitude
In effect, we descend to the lower pivotal altitude, and the pivotal altitude comes up to us
General Rule: If the point moves FORWARD, apply FORWARD pressure
As groundspeed increases, pivotal altitude increases as well
If no changes are made as the aircraft accelerates, it will be below the pivotal altitude
The wing will appear to move forward across the landscape
The point will move backward in relation to the wing
To compensate, the pilot must climb to maintain the reference line to the pylon
Airspeed decreases slightly, decreasing pivotal altitude
In effect, we climb to the higher pivotal altitude, and the pivotal altitude comes down to us
General Rule: If the point moves BACKWARD, apply BACK pressure
Corrections and Wind Speed
Corrections are like tracking a VOR
Once the correction is made (or an intercept angle is established), remove the correction when the pylon is back on the line-of-sight reference (or “intercepting the radial”)
Don’t make the correction and hold it
That will result in going above/below the pivotal altitude

sections.title: Changes in pitch/altitude are based on wind speed
sections.content:
Changes in pitch/altitude are based on wind speed
The greater the wind speed, the greater the variation in the max/min pivotal altitudes
Too strong of winds becomes unsafe
We get closer and closer to the ground
Also, the airplane can be blown very close to the pylon, requiring very high bank angles
RM: Uncoordinated flight								AI.IX.F.R5
This is the most common error in eights on pylons
Do not use the rudder to yaw the wing forward or backward to maintain the line-of-sight reference
Use altitude changes to hold the reference point on the pylon
Cross controlled flight is dangerous, especially close to the ground
Bank
Performed at bank angles ranging from shallow to steep (no more than 40o per the ACS)
The bank chosen does not alter the pivotal altitude
Distance from the pylon affects bank
As wind pushes the aircraft toward or away from the pylons, bank will have to be adjusted to maintain the reference line
If the pylon moves above your reference point (i.e. above the wing tip), the aircraft is banked too steep, should be decreased to maintain the reference
If the pylon moves below your reference point (i.e. below the wing tip), the bank is too shallow, and bank should be increased to maintain the reference
Note: Per the Airplane Flying Handbook, as proficiency is gained, the instructor should increase the complexity of the maneuver by directing the student to enter at a distance from the pylon that requires a specific bank angle at the steepest point in the pylon turn
RM: Energy Management & Power								AI.IX.F.R6
Pivotal altitude is based on groundspeed
Properly set power prior to entering the maneuver to keep the desired indicated airspeed consistent
Changes in power lead to changes in airspeed
Changes in airspeed will adjust the pivotal altitude and lead to changes in pitch
The more consistent the power setting, the more consistent the airspeed
This leads to a smoother maneuver that requires less work from the pilot
Reference Appendix A. Energy Management as needed for more detailed energy management concepts
Corresponding slides can be found in the slide’s appendix
Calculating Pivotal Altitude 									AI.IX.F.K3
Equation to estimate pivotal altitude
For Knots – ) + MSL
For MPH – () + MSL
Never going to be exact – use the planned true airspeed and estimated winds at altitude
Calculate the highest pivotal altitude: TAS + tailwind (highest groundspeed)
Use a flight computer
Take into account wind direction, speed, and true airspeed to get groundspeed
Calculate the lowest pivotal altitude: TAS – headwind (lowest groundspeed)
Remember that when in a headwind, we will be descending
Groundspeed will be slightly faster than planned and if the wind estimates are correct, we won’t get as low as expected
Calculating the highest and lowest pivotal altitude will provide an expected altitude window
If the altitudes are not safe, do not perform the maneuver
Performing Eights on Pylons 								AI.IX.F.K1, AI.IX.F.K5
Selecting the Pylons
Select two points on the ground along a line which lies perpendicular to the wind
The pylons should be:
Sufficiently prominent so the pilot can view them when completing the turn around one pylon and heading for the next
Adequately spaced to provide time for planning the turns but not spaced so far apart that they cause unnecessary straight-and-level flight between the pylons
The distance between the pylons should allow the straight-and-level segment to last 3-5 seconds
About ½ mile apart is a good estimate
The length of a small runway
At the same elevation, since differences over a few feet require climbing or descending between turns
In an open area and are not near hills or obstructions
The smaller the pylon, the easier to notice changes in movement (as long as you can see it)
RM: Emergency Landing Considerations							AI.IX.F.R7
Performed at low altitudes
There will be very little time and distance to glide to an emergency landing area
Select reference points in an area that provides for an emergency landing
Know what you will do and where you will go in the case of an emergency
Before the Maneuver
Pre-maneuver checklist
Ensure the area is clear of traffic
Below, at, and above your altitude

sections.title: The airplane should be trimmed for straight and level flight
sections.content:
The airplane should be trimmed for straight and level flight, at or below VA
Entering the Maneuver
Enter at a 45o angle to the downwind to make the first turn to the left around the left pylon
The left turn puts the pylon out the left window (easiest to see), rather than looking over the right seat passenger and through the right window
Make note of the entry heading as it will be the exit heading as well (bug the heading)
Fly to the midpoint between the pylons
A downwind entry starts with the highest groundspeed and therefore the highest pivotal altitude
Fly straight-and-level until the pylon is just ahead of the reference line, then roll into a 30o-40o bank
Not to exceed 40o
Place the wingtip at the base of the pylon
First Turn
Entry is at the highest groundspeed
Continuing through the turn, into an increasing headwind, groundspeed will get progressively slower
Pivotal altitude will decrease
If no corrections are made, the pylon will move forward of the wing tip
Forward movement = forward pressure
Descend to maintain correct pivotal altitude/reference point
Do not wait for the pylon to get significantly out of position, make consistent small corrections
Any airspeed gained in the descent increases pivotal altitude and helps correct the visual reference
Continuing the turn
Continuing the turn, groundspeed will begin to increase, and therefore pivotal altitude will increase
Climb to maintain pivotal altitude and the visual reference
If no corrections are made the pylon will move backward in relation to the wingtip
Backward movement = back pressure
Any airspeed lost in the climb decreases pivotal altitude and helps correct the visual reference
The relative wind will push the airplane towards the pylon 				AI.IX.F.K4
Bank angle will increase to maintain the visual reference
Remember, bank angle has no effect on pivotal altitude
No drift correction required since there’s no requirement to maintain a constant radius
Stay coordinated
Transitioning between Pylons
As the airplane turns toward a downwind heading, the rollout of the turn should be started
The airplane should proceed diagonally to a point on the downwind side of the 2nd pylon
Maintain straight and level flight for 3 to 5 seconds
Crab into the wind to correct for wind drift 							AI.IX.F.K4
The nose of the aircraft will have to point into the wind to properly correct for drift
The stronger the wind, the greater the correction required
Initiate a turn in the opposite direction when the pylon is aligned with the wing reference point
Second Turn
Entry is once again at the highest groundspeed, and therefore the highest pivotal altitude
As the turn continues, groundspeed decreases as the aircraft experiences more of a headwind
Pivotal altitude decreases
Descend to correct for changing groundspeed
The pylon will begin moving in front of the wingtip
Forward movement = forward pressure
Continuing the turn, the headwind will transition into more of a tailwind, and an increasing groundspeed
Increasing groundspeed = Increasing pivotal altitude
The pylon will move backward in relation to the wingtip
Backward movement = back pressure (climb)
Any airspeed lost in the climb reduces groundspeed and lowers the pivotal altitude
At this point, relative wind also pushes the airplane closer to the pylon 			AI.IX.F.K4
Bank must increase to maintain visual reference
Exit
After completing one rotation around each pylon, roll wings level, and exit on the entry heading
Common Errors 											AI.IX.F.K6
Failure to adequately clear the surrounding area for safety hazards, initially and throughout the maneuver.
Skidding or slipping in turns (whether trying to hold the pylon with rudder or not).
Excessive gain or loss of altitude.
Poor choice of pylons.
Not entering the pylon turns into the wind.
Failure to assume a heading when flying between pylons that will compensate sufficiently for drift.

sections.title: Failure to time the bank so that the turn entry is completed
sections.content:
Failure to time the bank so that the turn entry is completed with the pylon in position.
Abrupt control usage.
Inability to select pivotal altitude.
Hazards
Division of Attention 										AI.IX.F.R1
The entire maneuver is based on planning ahead (pivotal altitude), orienting yourself in relation to the wind and dividing attention between the aircraft, the reference points and what is coming next
Solid planning, starting with the pivotal altitude calculations on the ground, wind direction and reference point selection in the air, and smooth, proactive control inputs during the maneuver will make the eights on pylons much easier to perform
Poor planning results in a sloppy, considerably more difficult maneuver
Crosscheck should focus primarily on outside references with glances inside for airspeed, altitude, etc.
Over concentration inside or outside will result in the other being neglected and a poor maneuver
Allows the pilot to divide attention between aircraft control and the orientation
Orientation does not just include the bank angle/pitch attitude, but also where you are (airspace, terrain, etc.) and what or who is around you (aircraft, airports, etc.)
In the case of an unsafe situation or orientation stop the maneuver and fix the problem. Safety first
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 						AI.IX.E.R4
Distractions
They’re dangerous: Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance and clear for traffic
If distracted, recognize it and fix it – Safety first
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it and fix the problem
If disoriented, stop what you’re doing and get to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Management
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.IX.E.R3
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Be aware of, and avoid, obstructions, towers, etc.
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially slow, can result in a stall or loss of control close to the ground
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin
A spin is a result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Stop whatever you’re doing and recover at the first sign of a stall
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
Once the spin has stopped, neutralize the rudders and raise the nose, avoiding a second stall
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain)
AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground

sections.title: X.I. Spin Awareness & Spins
sections.content:
X.I. Spin Awareness & Spins
References: 14 CFR Part 23, Type Certificate Data Sheet; Stall and Spin Awareness Training (AC 61-67), Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
Who WANTS to do a spin? Most people fear spins but understanding them will help in avoiding them and remove some of the fear.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
A spin is an aggravated stall that results in what is termed “autorotation,” wherein the airplane follows a downward corkscrew path.
Why
An understanding of spins and the proper procedures to recover from them is necessary for safety. Understanding spins also increases confidence and reduces the anxiety associated with spins.
How:
Spins & Anxiety 										AI.X.I.K1, AI.X.I.K5
Spins are scary
A common perception to those unfamiliar with aviation is that a spin is a death sentence
They’re scary even to a lot of pilots, BUT we’re going to set you up for success with knowledge and training
To get into a spin, you have to stall the aircraft
Through your training, the intent is that you never unintentionally encounter a stall, but in the case that you do, you’re confident and capable of recovering
From there, the intent is that you’re so well trained that even if you do unintentionally encounter a stall, you never encounter a spin
And, in the unlikely event that the first 2 lines of defense fail, you will know how to recover from a spin
Knowledge and training can remove the anxiety and make you a far safer and competent pilot
Spin Aerodynamics 											AI.X.I.K3
Requirements for a Spin
A spin occurs when the wings exceed their critical AOA (stall) with a sideslip, or yaw, acting on the airplane
There are two requirements for a spin:
A stall
Yaw
Can be for any reason (rudder, adverse yaw, engine/prop effects, wake turbulence, etc.)
The yaw can occur at or beyond the actual point of stall
Basically…
In a spin, the inboard, low wing is more stalled than the outboard wing, which creates an autorotation, or rolling, yawing, and pitching motion around the vertical axis
Specifically…
When the aircraft stalls, one wing drops (the wing will drop in the direction of the yaw)
Although both wings are stalled…
The wing that drops has an increasing angle of attack (more stalled)
Lift decreases and drag increases on this wing
And the rising wing has a decreasing AOA (less stalled)
Lift increases and drag decreases on this wing
The autorotation results from the unequal angle of attack on the airplane’s wings
The difference in lift between the wings results in the rolling action
The difference in drag between the wings results in the yawing action
The load factor during a spin varies with the spin characteristics of each aircraft but is usually found to be slightly above the 1G of level flight. There are two reasons for this:
Airspeed in a spin is very low, usually within 2 knots of the unaccelerated stall speed
An aircraft pivots, rather than turns, while it is in a spin
4 Phases of a Spin
Entry Phase
The pilot intentionally or accidentally provides the elements for the spin (stall + yaw)
Incipient Phase
Occurs from the time the aircraft stalls and starts rotating to the time the spin has fully developed
Take approximately 2-4 turns for most aircraft
The aerodynamic and inertial forces have not yet balanced
Indications
Indicated airspeed will generally stabilize at a low and constant airspeed
The airplane in the turn indicator will indicate the direction of the turn
Keep in mind that the slip/skid ball is unreliable when spinning
Developed Phase
Occurs when the airplane’s angular rotation rate, airspeed, and vertical speed are stabilized in a flightpath that is nearly vertical
The spin is in equilibrium – the airplane’s attitude, angles, and self-sustaining motions about the vertical axis are constant or repetitive, or nearly so
Recovery Phase
Occurs when rotation ceases, and the AOA of the wings is decreased below the critical AOA
Various Factors & Spins (Very similar to info in the Stall lessons since a stall leads to a spin) 		AI.X.I.K2
A stall can occur at any airspeed, attitude, or power setting, depending on the total factors affecting the aircraft
Power Settings
Low Speed and/or Low Power Setting
As airspeed decreases, AOA must be increased to maintain altitude
Eventually, an AOA is reached that results in the wing stalling because the AOA has exceeded the critical angle and the airflow over the wing is disrupted
Increased load factor only exacerbates the slow, high AOA aircraft
High Speed and/or High-Power Setting
As discussed above
Depending on the aircraft, a higher power setting may reduce stall speed and increase lift on the wings
Although the wing may be stalled, a higher power setting can provide increased lift due to the propeller airflow/prop wash moving over the wing roots
More prominent in low wing aircraft where the propeller airflow moves directly over the wing
This airflow also likely has a relatively low angle of attack
Increased power at slow airspeeds and high angles of attack results in increased left turning tendencies
Anticipate considerable right rudder to maintain coordination

sections.title: Extremely important in preventing a spin
sections.content:
Extremely important in preventing a spin
Configuration
Flaps
Reduce the stall speed of an aircraft
Most flaps increase the camber of the wing and change the chord line, producing more lift
The nose is lowered to maintain altitude
Generally, the additional lift/lowered nose assist in decreasing the stall speed
Factors will vary based on aircraft/flap design
Note the differing speeds on the airspeed indicator (green arc vs white arc)
Flaps do not protect from an accelerated stall
Lower designed g-loads in flap configurations could lead to failure/damage
Gear – the effects of gear can vary based on the aircraft design and characteristics
Big picture, gear increases drag
Load Factor
Increased load factor increases the stall speed
Load factor is the ratio of the total load acting on the aircraft to the gross weight of the aircraft
Expressed in terms of Gs
Any increase in the load factor increases the stall speed
The stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor
When an aircraft is stalled at a higher than indicated air speed due to excessive maneuvering loads, it is called an accelerated maneuver stall
Pulling out of a steep descent, steep turns, aggressive control inputs, etc. Anything that puts Gs on the aircraft can increase the load factor and therefore the stall speed
Bank Angle & Load Factor
Increased bank angle increases the stall speed
Increased load factors are a characteristic of all banked turns
Tremendous loads are imposed as bank is increased beyond 45o
At a 60o bank, a load factor of 2 Gs is imposed on the airplane structure
At a 70o bank, a load factor of approximately 3 Gs is placed on the airplane
At approx. 63o of bank the stall speed is increased by approximately one-half
Weight
As the weight of the aircraft is increased, the stall speed increases
Remember, to maintain altitude lift must equal weight
So, the greater the weight, the greater the lift required
A higher AOA is required to generate the lift (all other factors remaining the same)
The higher AOA puts the aircraft closer to the critical AOA; thus, the aircraft will stall at a higher speed
A lighter aircraft will stall at a slower airspeed
Same as above, but opposite. Less lift is required, and the AOA can be reduced (all other factors remaining the same), lowering the stall speed
Center of Gravity
Forward Center of Gravity (CG)
Increases the stall speed
A forward center of gravity has the same effect on stall speed as a heavier aircraft
The farther forward the center of gravity moves, the higher the angle of attack has to be to compensate for the extra load imposed by the tail (see picture)
Due to the higher AOA, the aircraft is closer to the critical AOA and therefore will stall at a higher speed
More controllable due to the longer arm from the CG to the elevator - improves stall recovery
The farther forward the CG, the greater the tendency for the nose to pitch down
Imagine it as more “nose heavy”
Worth noting:
The higher AOA and increased deflection of the stabilizer increases drag; thus the aircraft is slower for a given power setting
Aft CG
Decreases the stall speed
An aft center of gravity has the same effect on stall speed as a lighter aircraft
The farther aft the CG, the lower the AOA has to be to compensate for the load imposed by the tail
Due to the lower AOA, the aircraft is farther from the critical AOA and will stall at a lower speed
Although stall speed is lower, the aircraft is less controllable due to the shorter arm from CG to elevator
Shortened arm produces less force making recovery more difficult
As the CG moves aft, recovery from a stall becomes progressively more difficult
Additionally, the farther aft the CG, the less tendency for the nose to pitch down on its own
Imagine it as more “tail heavy”
Worth noting:
The lower AOA and less downward deflection of the stabilizer reduces drag; thus, the aircraft is faster for a given power setting
Snow, Ice, and Frost
Increase the stall speed
Snow, ice and frost disrupt the smooth flow of air over the wing causing the boundary layer to separate at an angle of attack lower than the critical angle of attack
To make matters worse, lift is greatly reduced due to the disrupted air, and if ice accumulates, the weight of the aircraft is increased
More lift is required due to the added weight, but less lift is available due to the ice
As little as .8 millimeters of ice on the upper wing increases drag and reduces lift by 25%
Yaw Effects
Uncoordinated flight is what results in a spin
Stall + Yaw = Spin
Maintaining directional control and preventing the nose from yawing before stall recovery is initiated is key to averting a spin
Pilot must apply the correct amount of rudder to keep the nose from yawing and the wings from banking
RM: Spin Situations 									AI.X.I.K7, AI.X.I.R1
A Stall + Yaw = Spin
Any situation in which you have both a stall and yaw
During a go-around or short field takeoff
High pitch attitude, high power setting, and low airspeed situations
Turn from base to final
Cross controlled situation to avoid overshooting the runway without using excessive bank

sections.title: The spin that occurs from cross controlling an aircraft usua
sections.content:
The spin that occurs from cross controlling an aircraft usually results in rotation in the direction of the rudder being applied, regardless of which wingtip is raised
Sloppy stall recovery while practicing maneuvers
Unrecognized Stall Conditions
RM: Stall Warning Range & Limitations 		 					AI.X.I.R2
Buffet: Tends to occur prior to the stall horn
Generally, an early indication of a stall
May not always occur (Ex: Cross controlled stalls can occur with little to no warning)
Design, attitude, configuration, etc. preventing turbulent air from the wings hitting the stab
Stall Horn
Designed to provide warning of an approaching stall and time for stall recovery
Per 23.207
Clear/distinct stall warning with flaps & gear in any normal position, in straight and turning flight
Warning must begin at least 5 knots above stall speed and continue until the stall occurs
Must provide the pilot time to take action to avert the stall
Stall indications and horns have different operational ranges and limitations
Reference the POH for specific information
Ex: Uncoordinated flight may inhibit airflow at the stall indicator
Situations where one wing (without the indicator) stalls first
Recognizing Potential Spins 									AI.X.I.K10
Be aware of situations where a spin is most likely to occur
Understand what causes a spin and avoid those situations
A spin is dependent on yawing during a stall – Maintain coordination
Continued stall/spin recovery practice makes the pilot more competent in recognizing and avoiding a spin
Intentional Spins  											AI.X.I.K6
DO NOT intentionally spin an aircraft that is not authorized for spins
To determine if spins are approved check:
Airworthiness Category
Type Certificate and Data Sheets
AFM/POH – Limitations section
Placard in the airplane stating, “No acrobatic maneuvers including spins approved”
In the case spins are approved, also check:
Weight and Balance limitations
Recommended entry and recovery procedures
If the airplane is not certified, DO NOT attempt spins
Sometimes people will try to justify the maneuver
Technicality in the Airworthiness Standards
They say that the airplane was spin tested during certification
Normal Category classification only requires that an airplane recover from a one-turn spin of not more than one additional turn or 3 seconds, whichever takes longer
One 360o rotation does not provide a stabilized spin, therefore prolonged spins in that aircraft could be difficult or impossible to recover from
14 CFR Part 23
There are no requirements for investigation of controllability in a true spinning condition for normal category airplanes
The one turn margin is a check of the controllability in a delayed stall (not spin) recovery
Therefore, in airplanes placarded against spins, there is absolutely no assurance that recovery from a fully developed spin is possible
Weight and Balance Requirements
In airplanes approved for spins, compliance with weight and balance requirements is extremely important for safe performance and recovery from a spin maneuver
Even minor weight and balance changes can affect the airplane’s spin recovery characteristics
An aircraft that cleanly recovers from a prolonged spin with the CG at one position may fail completely to respond to normal recovery attempts when the CG is moved aft by one or two inches
An aircraft approved for spins in the utility category, but loaded in accordance with the normal category, may not recover from a spin that is allowed to progress beyond one turn
It is common practice for aircraft designers to establish an aft CG limit that is within one inch of the Normal Category maximum, which allows normal recovery from a one-turn spin
When certificating an aircraft in the utility category to permit intentional spins, the aft CG limit is usually established at a point several inches forward of that permissible for certification in the normal category
Spin Procedures 											AI.X.I.K1
Preflight
Perform a thorough preflight inspection with special emphasis on:
Excess or loose items that may affect weight, CG, and controllability
Within CG limitations
Slack or loose cables (especially rudder/elevator) could prevent recovery
Pre-Maneuver 											AI.X.I.K8
*Checklist - Fuel Pump ON; Mixture RICH; Lights ON; Gauges GREEN
Clear the Area - Above and Below
Altitude – CFI ACS: Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 4,000’ AGL
Airplane Flying Handbook: Begin at an altitude high enough to complete recovery at or above 1,500’ AGL
First turn results in an altitude loss of about 1,000’, each subsequent turn is about 500’
Maneuver
Entry Phase
Where the pilot provides the necessary elements for the spin (accidentally or intentionally)
Procedure (like a power off stall)
Reduce power to idle while simultaneously raising the nose to a stalling pitch attitude
As the stall approaches, smoothly apply full rudder in the direction of desired spin while applying full (to the limit) back elevator pressure
Keep the ailerons neutral
Maintaining a Stabilized Spin 								AI.X.I.K9
Maintain the above control inputs (yaw + stall)
Full back elevator pressure (stall)
Full rudder in the direction of the spin (yaw)
Neutral ailerons
Maintaining Orientation During a Spin 							AI.X.I.K11
Select an outside reference point
Use the turn coordinator

sections.title: The turn coordinator deflects in the direction of the spin a
sections.content:
The turn coordinator deflects in the direction of the spin and is reliable
Gyroscopic Instruments may tumble and be misleading (heading indicator, attitude indicator)
Incipient Phase
From the time the airplane stalls, and rotation starts until the spin has fully developed
Incipient spins that are not allowed to develop into a steady-state spin are most often used in the initial spin training/recovery techniques
May take to 2-4 turns for most aircraft
The aerodynamic and inertial forces have not reached a balance
Indicated airspeed should be near/below stall speed and the turn coordinator will indicate the direction of the spin
Developed Phase
Occurs when the airplane’s angular rotation rate, airspeed, and vertical speed are stabilized while in a flightpath that is nearly vertical
Aerodynamic forces and inertial forces are in balance, the spin is in equilibrium
Important to Note:
Some training airplanes will not enter into the developed phase but could transition from the incipient phase to a spiral dive
In this case, the airplane will not be in equilibrium but instead will be accelerating and as a result, G load can rapidly increase
In a spin, the airspeed does not accelerate
RM: Recovery Phase (PARE Acronym – Power, Ailerons, Rudder, Elevator) 	AI.X.I.K4, AI.X.I.K12, AI.X.I.R3
Occurs when the AOA of the wings decrease below the critical AOA and autorotation slows
Then, the nose steepens, and rotation stops – this phase may last ¼ of a turn to several turns
Note: Always follow the manufacturer’s procedures. In the absence of the manufacturer’s procedures, the recovery procedures below are recommended in the Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 4.
Step 1 – POWER IDLE
Power aggravates the spin characteristics, resulting in a flatter spin and increased rotation
Step 2 – AILERONS NEUTRAL
Ailerons may have an adverse effect on recovery
Aileron in the direction of the spin may speed rotation, steepen spin attitude, & delay recovery
Ailerons opposite the spin may cause flattening of the spin attitude and delayed recovery, or may even be responsible for causing an unrecoverable spin
Step 3 – RUDDER OPPOSITE THE ROTATION
Apply and hold FULL (to the stop) rudder opposite the direction of rotation until rotation stops
Rudder is the most important control for recovery in typical, single-engine airplanes, and its application should be brisk and full
Avoid slow and overly cautious opposite rudder which can allow the airplane to spin indefinitely
Step 4 - ELEVATOR FORWARD
To break the stall, apply a positive/brisk, straight forward movement of the elevator
Perform this step immediately after full rudder application – Don’t wait for rotation to stop
Hold the controls firmly in this position
This will decrease the AOA and break the stall (spinning will stop when broken)
Note: If airspeed is increasing, the airplane is no longer in a spin
In the spin, the indicated airspeed is relatively low, constant/not accelerating
Step 5 – RUDDER NEUTRAL
Neutralize the rudder after the rotation stops
If not neutral the increased airspeed will cause a yawing or skidding effect
Also, if the stall is not broken and full rudder is held in the opposite direction a spin can quickly start in the direction of the rudder pressure
Step 6 – ELEVATOR BACK PRESSURE
Once broken, raise the nose to level flight - Be careful of a secondary stall and exceeding load limits
Avoid aggressive movements resulting in an accelerated stall or a secondary stall
Do not leave the aircraft in a nose low attitude while altitude decreases, and airspeed increases
Common Errors (AFH 5-21) 										AI.X.I.K13
Failure to apply full rudder pressure (to the stops) in the desired spin direction during spin entry
Failure to apply and maintain full up-elevator pressure during spin entry, resulting in a spiral
Failure to achieve a fully stalled condition prior to spin entry
Failure to apply full rudder (to the stops) briskly against the spin during recovery
Failure to apply sufficient forward-elevator during recovery
Waiting for rotation to stop before applying forward-elevator
Failure to neutralize the rudder after rotation stops, possibly resulting in a secondary spin
Slow and overly cautious control movements during recovery
Excessive back-elevator pressure after rotation stops, possibly resulting in secondary stall
Insufficient back-elevator pressure during recovery resulting in excessive airspeed
RM: Hazards
Environmental Elements 									AI.X.I.R4
Turbulence
Can increase the stall speed
Sudden changes in relative wind, and/or aggressive control inputs can exceed the critical AOA
In moderate to severe turbulence or strong crosswinds, use a higher-than-normal approach speed
When flying below minimum drag speed (L/DMAX) the aircraft exhibits speed instability
If disturbed by turbulence and airspeed decreases, drag increases, leading to further loss of speed
Total drag continues to rise, and airspeed continues to fall
Microbursts
Can induce windspeeds greater than 100 knots and downdrafts as strong as 6,000 fpm
Depending on strength, climb ability can be minimized if not eliminated
Instinct can be to pitch excessively to counter the descent and avoid ground contact
Can quickly lead to a stall making the problem far worse than it already is
In the case of potential ground contact, increase pitch to minimize sink while avoiding a stall
Do not fly in or around thunderstorms or heavy rain showers where microbursts are most common
The best risk mitigation starts with effective planning
In the case of a microburst follow the POH procedures
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28)
See Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for details on recognizing/avoiding microbursts, and strategies for escape
High Density Altitude
Atmospheric Pressure

sections.title: Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affect
sections.content:
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affecting density
Changes in air density affect performance - As density increases, performance increases & vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)? Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Altitude, and Humidity
Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with temperature – As temp increases, density decreases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases and vice versa
How it affects Performance
As the air becomes less dense, it reduces:
Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is being moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils
Collision Hazards 										AI.X.I.R5
Collision Avoidance
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Execute gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind
Clearly communicate intentions & location in practice areas
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Divide attention between flying and scanning for aircraft
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program)
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
When aircraft of the same category are converging, the aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
If the aircraft are different categories:
Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over all engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final approach have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
Do not take advantage of this to force an aircraft off the runway which has already landed
When two or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of this rule to cut in front of another aircraft
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: An altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Over Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Over other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles and Wire Strike
Antenna Towers can extend over 1,000’-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which can extend 1,500’ horizontally from the structure
Overhead Wires (may not be lighted)
Overhead transmission wires and lines span runway departures and landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, & Task Management						AI.X.I.R6
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Sterile cockpit procedures
Focus on performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem, and fix it
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important – Lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
“Attack the closest alligator” – handle the most pressing problem and go from there
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate

sections.title: Conclusion:
sections.content:
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
Spins can be dangerous, especially when close to the ground. Understanding the reasons a spin can happen and how to prevent one is extremely important. If coordination is maintained during a stall, a spin will not occur. Once in a spin, recovery is accomplished by PARE - power to idle, neutral ailerons, full opposite rudder along with forward elevator pressure to break the spin. The recovery should be performed with brisk, positive pressure.

keyTakeaways: References: 14 CFR Part 23, Type Certificate Data Sheet; Stall and Spin Awareness Training (AC 61-67), Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Airspeed in a spin is very low, usually within 2 knots of the unaccelerated stall speed
Various Factors & Spins (Very similar to info in the Stall lessons since a stall leads to a spin) 		AI.X.I.K2

sections.title: XII.C. Systems and Equipment Malfunctions
sections.content:
XII.C. Systems and Equipment Malfunctions
Select the aircraft Systems and Equipment Malfunctions lesson from the Navigation Pane, or use the links below:
GENERIC
Generic Aircraft Malfunctions
CESSNA
Cessna 152
Cessna 172S G1000
CIRRUS
Cirrus SR20
DIAMOND
Diamond DA20
Diamond DA40
PIPER
Piper Archer II (PA-28-181)
Piper Archer III (PA-28-181)
Piper Arrow (PA-28R-201)
XII.C. Generic
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
Wouldn’t it be fun to be flying one day and experience a problem that you have no idea how to deal with? Of course not, that’s why it’s important to understand your equipment and the proper procedures associated.
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
Systems and equipment malfunctions involve the knowledge and procedures to handle problems that may occur in the airplane.
Why
The key to successful management of an emergency, and/or preventing a non-normal situation from progressing into a true emergency, is a thorough knowledge of, and adherence to, the necessary procedures.
How:
Note: This lesson provides generic procedures & malfunction discussions. Always follow the POH procedures.
Malfunction Procedures (MATL)
Maintain Aircraft Control
Fly the airplane
Get to a safe flight state (straight-and-level, etc.)
Trim the aircraft and turn on the autopilot, if possible
Maintaining control continues throughout the malfunction
Do not let the issue, checklists, etc. distract from flying the airplane
Divide attention between flying and checklists/procedures
RM: Distractions can lead to an undesired aircraft state (UAS) 				AI.XII.C.R4
Can quickly amplify the malfunction already being dealt with
The malfunction could also be the reason for the UAS
Maintaining control is the top priority – in the case of an UAS:
Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize as required
Understand the specific malfunction may limit or prevent recovery
Further emphasizes the need to maintain control
Analyze the Situation
Indications, lights, sounds, visual (i.e., smoke, leaks, fire, etc.), smells, etc.
Use all available information to determine the issue
Take the Proper Action
Apply any memory items
RM: Checklist usage – Use the appropriate checklist from the POH 				AI.XII.C.R2
Checklist is the safest, most effective way to handle the problem
Don’t go rogue and make up your own procedure/guess
Potential to not fix the problem and/or cause other problems
Land, as conditions require/permit
Based on the emergency, decide on a landing area (divert, field, ditching, etc.)
This may have to occur in conjunction with the checklist(s)
Power Loss 												AI.XII.C.K1
Rough running engine:
Oil Pressure Malfunctions
High Oil Pressure
Possible Cause - Cold oil or possible internal plugging
Corrective Action - If cold, allow the engine to warm, if not, reduce power and land ASAP
Low Oil Pressure
Possible Cause – Broken pressure relief valve, insufficient oil, burned out bearings
Corrective Action – Land as soon as possible or feather the propeller and stop the engine (multi-engine)
Fluctuating Oil Pressure
Possible Cause – Low oil supply, loose oil lines, defective pressure relief valve
Corrective Action – Land as soon as possible or feather propeller and stop engine (multi-engine)
Engine Overheat
The oil temperature gauge is the primary instrument in determining if the engine is overheating
Fuel Starvation
Normally indicated by a rough running engine, and can be caused by blocked lines or empty tanks
In general, turn on boost pumps, switch tanks, verify fuel is on, adjust mixture
Electrical Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2a
Electrical Power
Generally, power comes from a generator or alternator
If the generator/alternator fails, typically a battery provides power for a limited amount of time
Battery Time
The higher the amperage load (electrical draw) on the battery, the faster the energy gets consumed
Ex: 25-amp hour battery can produce 5 amps per hour for 5 hours
Increasing to 10 amps, it may only last 2 hours
40 amps may discharge the battery in 10-15 mins
Battery condition matters
Over time, power is reduced due to internal resistance
Very important to shed non-essential loads to provide maximum time
Consumers
See picture to right for average amperage
Gear and flaps use significant amounts of power
Using them may result in a total loss of power
Procedures
Follow the applicable checklist(s) in the POH
Reduce electrical load
Fly on the backup instruments
Generic Steps
Shed all but the most necessary electrical equipment
Can vary based on the situation (day/night, VMC/IMC)
Notify ATC immediately – Request vectors for landing at the nearest suitable airport
Expect a no-flap landing and manual gear extension
Vacuum/Pressure Malfunctions 									AI.XII.C.K2b
What’s Lost?
Heading Indicator, Attitude Indicator, and/or Turn Coordinator
Traditionally, turn coordinators use a different power source than the heading / attitude indicators
Ex. Vacuum for the attitude and heading gyros, and electric for the turn coordinator
If the heading & attitude indicators fail, the turn coordinator is still usable, and vice versa
Failure results from a loss of the suction or pressure source (vacuum failure)
As the gyroscopes slow down, they will begin to wander, displaying incorrect information
Can be slow and insidious
Many small aircraft do not have a warning system for vacuum failure
Look for vacuum failure indications – monitor the vacuum pressure gauge
Compare the Attitude Indicator with the Turn Coordinator and VSI
Along with providing pitch / bank information, this compares the static, suction, and electric systems
Identify the failed component(s) and use the remaining functional instruments to maintain control
Assess the situation - when and where to land may vary based on the conditions and failure(s)
Day VMC with backup instruments may allow the pilot to return to their home field
Night, reduced visibility, or minimal horizon may require an emergency and landing at the closest field
Pitot Static Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2c
General
Errors in the ASI and VSI almost always indicate a pitot blockage, static blockage, or both
Moisture, ice, dirt, insects, etc. can cause a blockages
Always preflight the pitot tube and static ports
Blocked Pitot System
Pitot system measures the difference between ram air pressure in the pitot tube and static air pressure from the static port
Static pressure is vented to instrument casing
Ram air is connected to a diaphragm in the case
Ram air blocked, with drain hole open
Air already in the system vents through the drain hole and remaining pressure in the pitot tube drops to match the outside (static) air pressure
Airspeed decreases to zero as ram air pressure and static pressure become equal
Not an instantaneous drop, but happens quickly
Ram air blocked, and drain hole blocked
Big Picture
Airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter
Ram air pressure in the pitot tube is trapped
Accelerating/decelerating does not affect indications
Static pressure changes with altitude
In a climb
Ram air pressure remains constant
Static pressure decreases
Diaphragm expands, just like would happen with an increase in ram air pressure/acceleration
Airspeed increases as altitude increases
In a descent
Ram air pressure remains constant
Static pressure increases
Diaphragm contracts, just like would happen with a decrease in ram air pressure/deceleration
Airspeed decreases as altitude decreases
Airspeed acts like an altimeter, increasing in a climb and decreasing in a descent
Blocked Static System
Static system blocked, with pitot tube open
Airspeed operates but is inaccurate
When above the altitude where the static port(s) were blocked, airspeed indicates lower than actual
Trapped pressure is higher than normal for the altitude
When at a lower altitude, airspeed indicates higher than actual
Trapped pressure is lower than normal for that altitude
Altimeter freezes at the altitude where the block occurred
Vertical Speed shows a continuous zero indication
Alternate Static Source
Provides alternate source of static pressure in the case the primary becomes blocked
Normally inside the flight deck
Cabin pressure is lower than exterior pressure due to venturi effect of air flowing around the fuselage
Instrument indications when the alternate static source is used:
Altimeter indicates slightly higher than actual
Airspeed indicates greater than actual
Vertical speed shows a momentary climb and then stabilizes if altitude is constant
Electronic Flight Display (EFD) Malfunction 								AI.XII.C.K2d
In the case of an EFD failure, the system reverts to a composite, reversionary mode
Moving map is eliminated
PFD and engine instruments are combined on the remaining screen
Pilots often become overly reliant on the moving map
What should be a supplementary source of data becomes a primary navigation tool
Significant loss of situational awareness if the pilot is not prepared for this failure
Stay Prepared
Follow the flight on an enroute chart while monitoring the moving map
Have a Chart Supplement to prevent losing access to airport information
Flap Malfunction 											AI.XII.C.K2e
Total Flap Failure (no flap approach and landing)
Requires substantially more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)
Losing altitude is more difficult so a wider, longer pattern may be necessary
Flown in a relatively nose-high attitude compared to flaps extended
On final, this can make it difficult to see the runway
Can lead to errors in judgement of height/distance and cause the perception the plane is close to a stall
Landing
Airplane is slightly less stable in pitch and roll axes with power reduced and flaps retracted
Tend to float during roundout
Don’t force the plane onto the ground
Don’t flare excessively as it risks a tail strike
Asymmetric (Split) Flap
A situation in which one flap deploys or retracts while the other remains in position
Indicated by a roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection
Countered with opposite aileron
Yaw caused by the additional drag on the extended flap side requires opposite rudder
Almost full aileron may be necessary at reduced airspeeds to maintain wings level
Do not attempt to land with a cross-wind from the side of the deployed flap
Be aware of the differing stall speeds of each wing
The wing with the retracted flap will stall earlier - possible cross-controlled stall condition
Approach and landing should be flown at a higher-than-normal airspeed
Hydraulic Malfunction  										AI.XII.C.K2e
If the hydraulic pump were to fail, there are alternate means to raise/lower the gear
Some airplanes will automatically lower the gear
Landing Gear Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K2e
Alternate gear extension procedure
If this does not solve the problem, a gear up landing is required
Considerations
Airport with crash and rescue facilities
A smooth, hard runway surface tends to cause less damage than a rough, unimproved grass strip
The hard surface does create sparks that could ignite fuel
Can request for the runway to be foamed, if available
Burn off excess fuel
Reduced landing speed and chance of fire
If the malfunction is limited to one leg, consume as much fuel from that side as practicable
Reduced weight on that side allows you to delay contact with the surface until the last moment
Reduced impact speed = reduced damage
Landing the Airplane
One Leg Retracted
Land in a nose-high attitude with wings level
As airspeed slows, apply aileron to keep the unsupported wing airborne as long as possible
After touchdown, the airplane will veer strongly in the direction of the faulty gear leg/dragging wing
Use full opposite rudder and aggressive braking to maintain some degree of directional control
On a narrow runway, or one with ditches/obstacles on the edges, landing with all gear up may be safer
Nose Wheel Retracted
Hold the nose off the ground until almost full-up elevator is applied
Release back pressure to allow the nose to slowly settle to the surface
Applying full back pressure results in the nose abruptly dropping to the surface
Can result in burrowing and/or additional damage
Try to gently set the nose on the ground
Do not apply brakes unless necessary to avoid a collision with obstacles
Main Gear Retracted (Nose extended)
Initial contact should be made on the aft fuselage with a nose high attitude
Helps to prevent porpoising and/or wheelbarrowing
Allow the nose-wheel to gradually touchdown
Use nose-wheel steering as necessary
Inoperative or “Runaway” Trim 									AI.XII.C.K2f
Grip the controls and maintain control of the plane while disengaging the electric trim system
Disengage button, circuit breaker, etc.
If the reason for the runaway trim is obvious and has been resolved, engage the breaker
Smoke & Fire  											AI.XII.C.K3
In any fire, it is essential the source is discovered first
Identifying the source allows the pilot to fight the fire most effectively
Identify/shutdown the faulty component, use the extinguisher effectively, run the proper checklist, etc.
In-Flight Smoke/Fire
Engine Fire
Usually caused by a failure allowing a combustible substance to contact a hot surface
Indicated by smoke / flames from cowling; and / or discoloration, bubbling, melting of cowling
Unless the POH says otherwise, 1st step should be to shut off fuel
If the flames are put out, do not attempt to restart the engine
Perform an emergency landing
Keep in mind:
There may be severe structural damage and control could be lost at any time
Airplane may still be on fire and susceptible to explosion
Airplane is expendable and the only thing that matters is the safety of those onboard
Electrical Fires
First indication is usually the distinct odor of burning insulation
Try to identify the problem by checking circuit breakers, lights, instruments, avionics
If it cannot be detected, the battery master and generator should be turned off
Any materials which have been ignited may continue to burn
If power is essential for the flight, attempt to identify / isolate the faulty circuit:
Electrical master off, then all individual electrical switches off
Electrical master on
Turn on electrical switches one at a time, waiting after each switch to check for signs of fire
Turn off / do not use any equipment that restarts the fire. Other equipment can be used
Cabin Fires
Usually result from smoking, electrical system malfunctions, and heating system malfunctions
Two immediate demands:
Attacking the fire, and getting the airplane safely on the ground as quickly as possible
In general, identify and shutdown the cause of the fire
Smoke can often be cleared by opening air vents – only after using the fire extinguisher
If smoke increases, immediately close them
Windows can also be used to help clear smoke
Use oxygen if the smoke is severe; initiate an immediate descent
Ground Smoke / Fire
Engine Fire / Smoke - Shut down the engine, turn off the electrics and evacuate the airplane
Electrical Fire / Smoke - Immediately turn off the master switch, and shutdown the engine
Use the fire extinguisher and evacuate as necessary
Door or Window Opening in Flight									AI.XII.C.K5
Follow the POH procedures. In general, adhere to the following:
Concentrate on flying the plane, an open door seldom compromises the ability of the plane to fly
Do not rush to land (climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern, make a normal landing)
Don’t release the seatbelt to attempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it
Most doors will not stay open, they will usually bang open then settle partially closed
A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away may push it closed
Pressurization Malfunction 										AI.XII.C.K4
Descend or use supplemental oxygen (emergency descent)
Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression
Other Malfunctions (supplemental oxygen, deicing, etc.) 						AI.XII.C.K4
Reference the POH and/or user’s manual for specific procedures
Common Errors 											AI.XII.C.K6
Inaccurate diagnoses of the malfunction
Use of an improper checklist/procedure
Lack of control throughout the malfunction
Fixation on the malfunction at the expense of the aircraft & safe flight
RM: Hazards
Startle Response										AI.XII.C.R1
Uncontrollable, automatic muscle reflex, raised heart rate, blood pressure, etc. elicited by exposure to a sudden intense event that violates a pilot’s expectations
Protect against startle response through scenario-based training incorporating realistic distractions
The pilot should react in a calm, controlled manner and:
Maintain aircraft control
Analyze the situation
Take the proper action
Land, as conditions require/permit
Reactions or inputs outside of checklists may likely aggravate the situation
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization		 				AI.XII.C.R3
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Focus on aircraft performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem and fix it
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Especially important to avoid distractions in an emergency with numerous tasks to manage
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
High task load during an emergency can lead to a loss of SA
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
Divide attention between inside and outside references
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft & malfunction, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention for more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Organization is especially important in situations like this – many tasks, little time
“Attack the closest alligator”
When tasks are piling up, handle the most threatening problem
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points
Understanding different emergencies and how to deal with them is obviously important as you will always be prepared and be able to react quickly in the event one of these emergencies occurs.
XII.C. DA20
References: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3), POH/AFM
